title: I Did It My Way... and Got Fired
author: Managing the Future
summary: This article argues that the trait most responsible for getting leaders to the CEO seat -- unshakeable self-confidence -- is also the trait most likely to get them fired once there. The author, who runs CEO Masterclasses, observes that D-type (Dominance) personalities make up roughly 70% of CEOs despite being only 9% of the population, and that this deeply-held self-reliance serves leaders well in functional executive roles but becomes dangerous at the top, where no one can be expert in everything. When confidence tips into overconfidence, CEOs stop listening, stop seeking outside perspective, and try to run the organization 'their way' -- exactly the behavior that leads boards and investors to lose confidence. The piece argues that real confidence at the CEO level means knowing what you don't know, cherishing disagreement, and giving up the idea that the CEO must be the source of all insight. The window for a new CEO to demonstrate momentum is narrow -- roughly 12 to 18 months -- and those who spend it doubling down on self-reliance rather than building team intelligence tend to fail fast.
points: * D-type personalities make up only 9% of the population but over 70% of CEOs -- and it is precisely this trait of unshakeable self-belief that becomes the CEO's greatest liability once they are in the role. * The CEO job is categorically different from any prior functional role: a VP of Sales has deep pattern recognition in a defined domain, but the CEO must make decisions across domains they have never run, often with 70% information and no 'right' answer -- only tradeoffs. * The feedback loop at the CEO level is slow and non-obvious, which means the window for bad judgment to compound is long, but the board's patience is short -- typically 12 to 18 months before confidence either builds or collapses. * The most important shift a CEO can make is to stop being 'the source of all insight' for the team and start receiving insight from the team -- asking 'What don't I know?' and actively cherishing employees who will disagree. * The CEO who says 'I'll do it my way' is applying to an organizational context a posture that is precisely the pathology that kills execution and leads to derailment.
quotes: Being confident is essential. You can't lead an organization through hard decisions and cut through all the ambiguity a CEO deals with unless you have a baseline trust in your own instincts. But that confidence can also be the most dangerous trait a CEO can have.

The problem is when self-confidence balloons into overconfidence. It's at this point that the CEO's inner voice starts saying things like: I know best. I'll figure it out myself. I'll do it my way. That instinct, left unchecked, is how smart executives fail as CEO.

If you rose through sales, you're used to having a playbook and a clear scoreboard. If you came up through finance or operations or engineering, you have deep expertise in that defined domain. You know how to solve the problems in your lane because you've spent years developing pattern recognition in that lane. The CEO job throws all of that out.

You're no longer the expert. You can't know everything. You need to make decisions that affect departments you've never run. There's no 'right' answer. There are only tradeoffs. The very trait that helped you rise to CEO -- the unshakeable commitment to your own instincts -- becomes an obstacle to getting the outside perspective you now genuinely need.

Give up the idea, likely held over from previous roles you held, that you must be the source of all insight for your team. Now, as CEO, you're the one who should be receiving the insights from your team. Ask people to play devil's advocate. Cherish the employees who will disagree with you. Be curious.

Most CEOs have a window of roughly 12 to 18 months to demonstrate momentum before the board, investors, or the market starts losing confidence. The feedback loop isn't tight though. It's hard to know if you're doing the right things.
